source.title: Why Larger Models Learn More: Effects of Capacity, Interference, and Rare-Task Retention
source.authors: Jing Huang; Daniel Wurgaft; Rachit Bansal; L. Ruis; Naomi Saphra; David Alvarez-Melis; Andrew Kyle Lampinen; Christopher Potts; E. Lubana

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies how model scale affects learning rare and complex tasks, but does not test the fall-rise-fall error patterns, interpolation-threshold peak, or sample-wise error increase in the claim versions. It mentions double descent in related work as a possible phenomenon for future investigation.
record.gate_note: The reported scaling results concern learning task-specific behavior, representation, and gradient interference. They do not establish or measure a double-descent curve. The paper also describes further results in figures and appendices; the rows below capture its explicit, relevant scaling findings rather than treating those as tests of double descent.
record.test_reason: The paper studies why larger models learn rare and complex tasks (synthetic multitask linear-bottleneck regression and OLMo 4M–4B with injected tasks). Its scaling curves are monotonic by design and it never measures test error through an interpolation threshold. Double descent appears only once, in Appendix A related work, as a question for future work on frequent tasks. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors give a data-centric account: larger models learn rare and complex tasks through reduced competition and gradient interference and better retention. They present it as complementary to expressivity and sample-efficiency accounts, not as a complete account of scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses synthetic multitask regression and injected-task OLMo pretraining to study rare-task learning and interference. It does not reproduce the original double-descent method or measure error around an interpolation threshold.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported learning outcomes depend on task frequency, task complexity, model width, and the gap between injected task batches.

fits_no_version.finding: In synthetic multitask regression, wider models learn lower-utility (rarer or more complex) task features, in the order predicted by frequency-weighted utility.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Width scaling lets a model learn lower-frequency task features that narrower models fail to learn, even when trained longer.

fits_no_version.finding: Under matched-frequency injection, wider or larger models retain rare-task signal between observations, while smaller ones decay to near zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger models retain rare-task updates across gaps between observations better than smaller models.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger OLMo models learn low-frequency injected tasks and represent more task features than smaller ones.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger OLMo models learn rare injected tasks and their features more effectively.

fits_no_version.finding: Non-task gradient alignment with the task direction is near zero for the 1B model, versus 0.10 ± 0.09 for the 20M model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger models show less gradient interference from non-task tokens on task neurons.

record.problems: The authors state that empirical validation in a realistic pretraining setting may leave analytic gaps; they did not test larger-scale or over-trained language models, and the selected injected tasks and frequency range may not cover other scaling behavior. The reported OLMo model-size evidence is limited to the stated 4M-to-4B range.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed additional frequency and complexity sweeps and plotted retention traces in Appendices D and E were not recorded separately; they provide further instances of the same rare-task learning and retention findings, not tests of the listed double-descent versions.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep of test error around the interpolation threshold; the width curves are monotonic, with fresh data each step.
No epoch-wise test-error curve is reported.
No capacity sweep past interpolation in any model class.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
No label noise, regularization tuning, or multiple-descent analysis.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only'. Double descent is mentioned only in one related-work sentence (refs 108–112) as a possible mechanism for future study, so no verdicts are given. The 20M model's non-task gradient similarity (0.10 ± 0.09) is in the text but not in the rows; it does not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep measures test error through a peak near the size that just fits the training set and a subsequent decline.
Training dynamics are reported for task learning and retention, not a fall-rise-fall test-error curve over epochs.
The study varies task frequency and injection gaps, not training sample count near an interpolation threshold with test error as the outcome.
The study does not test double descent across model classes or capacity past an interpolation point.
The paper analyzes feature utility and task frequency/complexity, not a single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across size, epochs, and samples.
The study does not test label noise, regularization-dependent double-descent peaks, or triple/multiple descent.
The study does not recount complexity using effective parameters or assess whether that transforms a second descent into a U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: linear-bottleneck student
rows.stage_stated: trained for 100K steps; longer runs up to 10× are also described
rows.operation_detail: Varied model width and measured per-task loss on the synthetic task mixture.

conditions.value: shared α = 2 in the main visualization

rows.measure: Per-task loss and overall residual loss
rows.baseline: Mean-predictor loss for the normalized per-task measure
rows.value: The paper states that per-task loss and overall residual loss reduce with width, and that larger models learn infrequent tasks better.
rows.note: This is a width-scaling result for task loss, not a reported test-error double-descent curve.
rows.check: Monotonic width-scaling of per-task loss in a linear-bottleneck student with fresh samples each step; there is no interpolation threshold, so it cannot show a double-descent peak. Link to none is correct.

rows.subject: linear-bottleneck student
rows.stage_stated: trained on the synthetic task mixture
rows.operation_detail: Varied width and measured task signal represented by the encoder.

conditions.value: most frequent and rarest tasks; frequent set has cumulative prior mass 0.8

rows.measure: Normalized task signal and residual common-task signal
rows.baseline: Random-representation signal baseline, corrected to 0 by the stated normalization
rows.value: The paper states that small models leave frequent-task residual signal and have rare-task signal no better than random; as width increases, frequent-task signal is explained and rare-task signal begins to be learned.
rows.note: Representation and task-learning outcome; not a measure of the claimed error curve.

rows.subject: linear-bottleneck student
rows.size_stated: multiple widths; exact widths not stated in the main-text description
rows.operation_detail: Withheld the rare task for G steps, then injected a batch of rare-task examples while matching its long-run frequency.
rows.measure: Rare-task signal retained between injections and at the end of training
rows.value: The paper states that rare-task signal decays with increasing G at all widths, more steeply for smaller models; larger models accumulate signal while smaller models decay to near zero between injections.
rows.note: This reports retention under a task-injection protocol, not epoch-wise test error.
rows.check: Retention of rare-task signal over training steps under an injection protocol. It is not a test-error curve over epochs, so it does not bear on V2.

rows.subject: OLMo models (4M, 20M, 300M, 1B, and 4B parameters)
rows.stage_stated: pretrained on Dolma v1.7 with injected tasks
rows.operation_detail: Compared task training loss and test accuracy across model sizes and injected-task frequencies.
rows.measure: Injected-task training loss and test accuracy
rows.value: The paper states that larger models learn lower-frequency tasks much better; only larger models at higher task frequency show the stated grokking behavior on TADD.
rows.note: The reported size effect concerns injected-task performance; it does not report a double-descent peak.

rows.subject: OLMo models
rows.operation_detail: Compared task learning order and task loss under matched-frequency injection with different gaps.
rows.measure: Task loss and order of task learning
rows.baseline: Reference arithmetic tasks from pretraining for the learning-order comparison
rows.value: The paper states that tasks are learned in frequency order and that larger gaps between injected instances increase task loss despite equivalent global task frequency.
rows.note: The gap manipulation concerns task retention, not a sweep over training sample count measuring test error.
rows.check: The injection-gap manipulation keeps total task frequency fixed; it does not vary sample count near interpolation, so it does not bear on V3.

rows.subject: OLMo models
rows.size_stated: model size varied; exact per-model results not stated in the text description
rows.operation_detail: Compared task-feature presence across model sizes and task frequencies.

conditions.value: comparison TCMP and modular addition TADD
varied; model-size comparison fixes frequency separately for each task

rows.measure: Task-feature representation: comparison-task feature fit and number of detected Fourier modes
rows.value: The paper states that larger models and models trained on more frequent task data learn the identified task features faster, and that feature presence correlates strongly with test accuracy.
rows.note: The measure is representation, not the error curve named in the claim.

rows.subject: OLMo 1B model
rows.operation_detail: Measured cosine similarity of batch gradients with a task-reference direction.
rows.baseline: Zero similarity is the stated reference for orthogonality
rows.value: Full-batch similarity is 0.08 ± 0.02 at injection steps; non-task gradient similarity is 7.58 × 10⁻⁵ ± 0.02.
rows.note: This is gradient-interference evidence, not a double-descent measurement.

relation.reason: Appendix A, p. 21, explicitly considers whether scaling could prevent frequent-task overfitting through double descent and proposes investigating that counterpart to its rare-task account.

tranche.reason: The study measures rare-task learning, retention and gradient interference; it neither tests a double-descent claim version nor uses double descent as a tool.

source_check.notes: The authors’ conclusion is accurately paraphrased. Gradient similarities concern selected neurons in the first-layer MLP; the 1B non-task similarity is 7.58 × 10−5 ± 0.02.
